To let me have some water?
How, my lord?
There is no jug will pour between the bars,
Nor any vessel.
I shall die of drought;
And the bread makes it worse. My lips are stiff
As clay in August. I can eat no more.
There, father, to your face!
Patience, my lord,
I cannot think he knows.
He's cast me off,
Prey to the thirst and hunger he has chained
Within me from my birth! He's slipped the leash!
Help me!
I'll do the utmost woman can.
There's Emmeline the armourer's wife.—Be sure
I'll help you if I can.
Then I shall live,
Live and be young again—perchance escape.
I will be patient—there's the sound of life
Within your voice; it wakens me. You've seen
The sun to-day, and I shall see 't again.
You've brought me hope.—I cannot talk.
Nay, nay.—
Bless me! His eyes still ask!—I'll come anon.

div.head: Scene III.
div.stage: —Another part of Falkland Castle. Enter Emmeline.

lg.l: Now sweet good soul ...
I must not speak with you.
'Tis pert for such as I to say a word;
But answer me one thing, good mistress, one,—
Have you not heard strange cries?
I thought the birds
Were noisy; but 'tis clearer and distressed.
I've heard it many times.
'Tis not the birds,
But a poor soul that's caged.
A prisoner?
Ay, mistress, an' they're clemming him to death.
If you could see him, mistress, look on him!
His hair is tattered like the yellow fern
On our December wolds; his cheeks—nay, hear!—
As snows in thaw are dwindled, an' he weeps.
He's but a youth, and, mistress, he's our prince.
Then let us help him.
I have ta'en him cakes—
You know how fine we make 'em, an' 'twas well
The prison-bars are close. I fairly quaked
To see his greed. But he is thirsty still.
We'll take him drink.
Alas, the bars are close
Beyond all hope, poor soul!
Can we do naught?
I cannot, mistress ... but—
You think I can.
I'm ready.
But you never will forgive
That I should tell you—
Do not frighten me,
Or say to me aught I must never hear.
What can I do?
Give what you gave the child ...
I speak it not in lewdness ... but your milk
Is all the charity that God will grant.—
I'll go away.
If you should wave your handkerchief, I'll come
An' take you to the place.
He is not pure.
None mention him with honour, and the woman
Who pleads for him hath lost her holy fame.
It may be she'd beguile my innocence,
And draw me into sin with pity's net.
But still it was not in her look or words;
For falsehood leaps not thus within the eyes,
Nor from the mouth springs forth; it ever comes
With tardiness and caution. She is true,
And then ... O woman's shrine on which God lays
A husband's faith and a babe's confidence,
White altar for Love's consecrated gifts,
Could Pity desecrate the pale retreat
Of modest wedded peace and motherhood?—
The milk is throbbing in my breast, to stay
The grief of hunger. Oh, I must not close
The fountain of God's mercy with rough pride,
For He will keep it holy, and the eyes
Of misery are pure. In our dread times
Of war and woe, too many are the veils
Raised from our easier days that I should shrink
To stir my clinging wimple. I will go.
He had a mother once, and as her child
I'll think of him and go.—My handkerchief.
The saints be with you!
Take me where I go.

div.head: Scene IV.
div.stage: —The same. A Dungeon. Rothsay and Emmeline.

lg.l: Do not leave me yet.—
I'm called.
You must not put me from the milk,
And leave me. God! I'm fed with innocence,
And like a baby fall upon my sleep.
Keep close!
My lord, lie down upon the ground;
It may be you will rest.
Ay, if you watch.
I cannot sleep alone.
The very air is starved and shrieks at me
For the want of human breath. Oh, let me feel
The succour of a voice. Put me to sleep
With some soft cradle-words.
My memory
Is crazed; I cannot think of them.
Oh, fly!
Mistress, be quick, there is the sound of steps.
Unless you watch me, Slumber will not come,
For I should be too secret to be found
Of one so blind. I cannot lay my hands
On any of my senses; all's confused;
All's lost. ...
I've got one little cake within my vest—
I shall forget where I have hidden it,
Unless you watch. It's growing dizzy now,
And you keep drawing back.
Lie down, my lord.
It's rest you need.
Oh, mistress, we are lost!
What! You are come again!
To bid good-night,
And settle you to sleep: you'll say your prayers?
I have no prayers; I'm back now to the child. ...
It's a land of milk and honey. ... Oh! I drowse. ...
Don't stir!
He's breathing heavily; he's gone.
They're on us!
He's asleep.
Now may I—

div.stage: [Enter Wright, Selkirk, with the Country Woman.]

lg.l: Hang!
For pity's sake, save her!
She's kind and young: 'twas I that forced her come
With story of the pain in yonder cell.
She came not of herself.
Nor by herself
Shall feel the noose. The gallows carries two,
Old nurse of Satan!
You are beasts, and worse
Because you look like men, to starve the child
Within there—pinch his bonnie youth and wring
Tears from his royal eyes; and then to hang
This dearie. ...
Ho! a cord! She'll deafen us.
Sly harlots!
He's spent everything on such.
Now 'tis your time to pay. He's bankrupt, lass.
These insults worse than kill me.
Hold your tongues,
You savages!
Old watch and bawd!
Ye heavens,
Make haste to end my hearing!
Off with them.
The deil! He's gone to sleep. Spite o' the bars,
You've charmed him.
When he wakes ... and oh! we're dead
I must not think.
He will not wake again.
Heaven bless you! he will wake in Paradise.
Ye murderers! you'll have it hot in hell.
God's mother, curse you!
Hush! we will not speak.
Let us die still.
Cords! cords!
Then gurgle out
Your devil's threats!
Oh! ... if my Henry comes,
He'll find me dead and learn about my death;
He will not like it here; but when he's taught
A little of the angels, he will smile
And take me to his arms. I'm ready now.

div.head: Scene V.
div.stage: —King Robert, and Prince James on the hearth, Albany, and the Duchess Marjorie.

lg.l: The wind is raging! it afflicts my head,
And stirs it to confusion.
A wild night
For those not warmly housed; of dark presage
To our camped soldiers if they couch to rise
To-morrow to a battle. As they lie,
Their death-shrieks like pale ghosts will stride to them
Across the wailing air, and—curse the fools!—
Unman them for the fray.
O Robert, peace!
I shudder.—Draw up nearer to the fire.
An ingle-nook is gracious at such hours,
When all are gathered round it.
Truth! The glow
Is pleasant, and doth ruddily assure
The heart of safety.
'Tis a black, black night.
D'you think it cold?
Scarcely for March.
And yet
The blaze is welcome.
'Tis a trifle chill
For those of fearful mind.
Then he is cold—
James, shall you be afraid to sleep to-night
In all this noisy darkness?
Father, no!—
I'm not afraid.—My noble hound, you've got
A comfortable ear.
The dauntless child!
Our army will be routed by the air
Before it face the English. May to-night
Find it within some guarded vale that's slow
To open gates and parley with the storm.
There snaps a limb of some aghasted oak!
The Devils make Inferno of our woods.
Hark! Listen!
Oh, I wonder if he wears
The little relic that his mother tied
About his neck.
I'm speaking of the troops—
Will David sleep like you?
He fears the dark.
And, father—
James, you're pressing on the dog.
His sides can scarcely bear your elbow-joint,
Though willing for your head.
Is he asleep?
No, no; not he! He's listening by the fire,
As we are, to the rattle out of doors.
Ah, as I told you, when my words were crashed
By falling of the oak, our army lies
In danger from the weather.
My poor lad,
My David, who is fearful of the dark,
Would he were here this bleak and scolding night!
He used to throw a cushion on the floor,
And lay him down as featly as the hound,
His foolish yellow head against my knee;
And so he'd laugh and chat and sing old songs,
Or gaily sneer at our last grave debate,
Drop sudden crude suggestions that anon
Our older counsel ripened into act;
Until for some light word I'd give rebuke,
When either with a peal of raillery
He'd toss me back a penitent bright face,
Or with a shaded humour spring apart,
No place from me too far. Good Albany,
You would not have our Rothsay longer shut
In such grim-tempered darkness?
Fifteen days!
'Tis but a slender punishment, my liege.
Enough, enough! The terror of this night
Doubles the term of his captivity,
And makes of it a month.
We'll send for him
Before the week hath touched its sacred goal.
By this he must be dead.
Why now I'm warm in spirit, which the fire
With all the urgent comfort of its face
Could not effect; I'll send for him anon.
How glad I am in soul! Yet I confess
I'm half afraid to meet him. Now all's well,
I'll think of him no more.
Your porridge, sire.
Put it away, I have no appetite;
The turmoil makes me disinclined to eat.
Good Allan, set it on the hearth and stir.
Have you all supped?
Why do you pace about?
My foot is gone to sleep.
When did you sup?
Like you, I have no stomach for a meal.
All that I eat is heavy in my throat,
As if I gulped the bait on Hell's own hook.
This rain will smear our army's pride.
Too sure.
Yet are the troopers hardy and rough-bred,
Trained by strict weather to all skiey chance,
And led by one whose buff coat of bull's hide
Enfeebles all the water of the clouds,
And makes it folly.
Black old Archibald!
Allan, he is a mountain, and his voice
A waterfall.—Give me that oaten lump
Upon your spoon.—There, dog!—another one!—
Mouth open!
Allan, stir the embers up;
They lay themselves to rest.
A blaze, a blaze!
Brave! They put out red tongues, and roar for food
Like the big lion.
But the wind is shrill
Above their noise.—What's that?
What?
Some one dies;—
Mother of Christ!—for look you at the dog;
He shivers as an ague, an' his whine
Is like a sinner's, drowning in hell's pitch.
The Banshee! Hark!
Allan is credulous.
'Tis an old story when the wind is sad,
And wails about a corner. By the tower
I've noted that it cries most audibly.
Ah, Allan! how you struck upon my fear,
And thumped on it as 'twere a crazy drum.
Brother, a woman is more rational
Than three old men.
Well, sire, I know the wind
Hath got no breast from which such grief can moan;
An' why, sire, should the dog be scared with things
That touch not man?
Nay, nay, but he is still.
Again, again! It is a voice, my God!—
You know it, Albany; your eyes are cow'd,
You cannot lift them, tho' you shake your head.
It calls me, calls!—Allan, you say the voice
Is full of death and direful prophecy.
O Allan! do you think you know its tones?
The same the blast makes ever when like Jews
It lifts its lamentations by a wall.
I think 'tis so.
Think, think! But is your thought
The very cause? or do the elements
Speak out what we are deaf to in our souls,
And force a hearing?
Should I know? How? why?
This is mere fooling. Mass! D' you think of me
As privy-counsellor to Doomsday, man!
It may be hurricane; it may be speech.
It is his voice!—Your shoulder, Albany—
Open the door! No matter if I fall.
Will it not open—never? Does it keep me
Like a tomb's gate eternally at stand?
Burst every lock!
David, my son, my son, thy father hears!
Thou shalt be freed, shalt come to me again.
Nothing shall hinder—chains, nor bars, nor bolts;
Nothing shall dare oppose my tyrant love
That binds and looses. David, thou art free
This moment. I have heard thee call, my son,
And all my soul hath answered thou art free.
Come in! The madness of this howling air
Hath made you its interpreter. Come in!
Let it rage on in accents of its own,
And give it not our language. Come away!
He calls no more; his misery is done,
For I have promised comfort and release.
This burthen on my shoulder is too much.
Brother, you lean
With desperate weight on me. A lighter hold!
Pr'ythee, to save my breath hang not so hard.
The very soul of hearing finds no sound,
No slightest human sigh in all this wind.
Now shall you in with me.
How dare you put
My son and I apart?
The wind convicts!
If you give ear
To a chance spasm in the air to fix
On me a guiltiness ...
There may be more.
They are possessed. I thought that Albany
Had nerve and reason stronger.
The king's hair
Flies round like foam; his breath is much distressed.
We must entreat him back,—an' yet to stir
Seems irreligious.
I will go. Stay here,
And I'll beseech him shut the door again.
Nothing! 'Tis gone; and yet I fancy still
It bleats upon the air.
No; on my soul,
All's over. ...
Stay!
I've said it audibly.
My lips have witness'd 'gainst me.
Father, sir!
You're cold and weak to bear this chilly gale.
Do not stay longer out.
I will not, boy.
James!
You are wise to move.

sp.speaker: King Robert.

lg.l: My child, your hand.
Albany, shut the door

sp.stage: [returns to his seat, led by Prince James]

lg.l: . And, boy, to bed!
It was the wind that shrieked.
Well, heard you aught
But windy fret and uproar?
If my liege
Will pardon, I'll go start a messenger
To Falkland, that your mind may be at peace.—
This wanton blast beguiles me. Conscience is
A fool o' the weather and the time o' night.—
I've your authority to send this man?
That of my fatherhood and royalty,
Which hand in hand instructs you so to do.
I will; and if we do not meet again—
As I'll retire to rest—good-night, my liege;
And keep your mind from brooding on the fears
Absence and Love, with magic craft combined,
Both sorcerers, have raised for us this eve.
Robin, good-night, if you can shift to sleep.
Cries in the whirl of night bode ...?
Nothing.
Death.
I think you are mistaken there—distress.
As you will, sire.
And are they near of blood,
Or even kin at all for whose decease
The air is said to toll?
I scarcely know.
But I should say for any fate hath put
Near to our int'rest, sire.
Then may this groan
For Douglas rive the throbbing atmosphere.
The army on whose welfare I have set
My nearest hopes may, at this very hour,
Perish in blood, their leader struck to earth,
With none to ring a dirge but senseless gusts.
He almost smiles. Ah! deepest selfishness
That would prefer the doom of honest souls,
Led by a great and high-deserving chief,
To loss of its own pampered libertine.—
My father by the law, you give to fate
Him, who by nature is my father's self.
I am his daughter; but I'm blunt in soul,
And you so tender-strung that, at all cost,
You get you comfort.
Oh, I'm base indeed
For such oblivion to cross my sense
As hid your dear relationship to him
I fancied slain.
Nay, I am used to such.
My girl, forgive me, for you cannot know
What it is works within a parent's breast;
'Tis the begetting makes the difference,
And so my passion grew.
Your subjects?

sp.speaker: King Robert.

lg.l: Hush!
This is all talk; we'll build no argument
On these disjointed rumours of the storm.
Your father is not bleeding. Cheerly, lass!
All's well.

sp.stage: [Exit Duchess Marjorie with a distant obeisance.

lg.l: 'Tis very quiet out of doors—
Unnatural!—I'll go and look at James.

div.head: Scene VI.
div.stage: —Same Apartment. Enter Walter, Randolph, and Allan.

lg.l: Nothing from Falkland?
Nothing.
From the wars?
Nothing.
An empty mouth, an empty mouth!
Better than have it filled with bitterness.
I look for no good news.
Thou croaking man,
Thou raven, soul of evil augury,
Wherefore bad news?
It is the feeling, man,
And the dull sky.
God bless your sense, I feel
As merry, ay, as merry as the morn,
The cricket, lark, or any earthly thing
That figures my condition; and the clouds
From sullen flash to gay as seconds pass,
So I can build my humour on the sky
As well as you.
You can, my chanticleer!
Marry, as thus: the prince will home again,
The king for very love will give him gold,
The gold will give us feast and merriment,
And jolly cups and wenches' jocund lips;
All these delights in turn will give us heart
To celebrate authentic victory
Of Scotland o'er the bragging English hinds.
O lads, defeat!
Come, come!—an ugly game!
We'll play at victory, if play we must.
Victoria!
All's over, all is lost;
Douglas a captive, with a gored right eye
And spouting wounds; our host but helpless limbs
And bleeding impotence that cannot meet
The wing'd attack of the mere birds of Heav'n.
The English Hotspur and our traitor March
Fell on the trustful bands, adorn'd with spoil,
And shook them to the nakedness of death.
Where fell the woful chance?
At Homildon.
Allan, thou wry-faced prophet, I have done!
The prince will next be either churchyard's corpse
Or church's convert. I will never speak
High-stomach'd language more.
How went the fight?
Why thus:—our Douglas, in audacious fit
(Foolhardy as his wont), in fated hour,
Bore up our army to a topping brow
Of moorland, naked, tree-unbonneted,
And open to the arrows' swift assault—
There held our men a target to the foe,
A troop for slaughter; till a voice arose
That thrill'd the pulseless manhood of our host
With surgent valour,—high it rose and clear
Above the whizzing darts, the foeman's yell,—
Higher, as if it scorn'd opposing sound—
John Swinton's knightly voice that cried aloft:
“Why stand we here as stags upon the hill,
Dart-stricken brutes, when down these drenchèd slopes
Naught hinders that we rush upon the foe
To fight as victors or to fall as men?”
They wake; they gather with a forward sway;
Death is forgotten, ay, and deadly feud;
For young lord Gordon, whose good sire was slain
By Swinton's hand, unmindful of revenge,
Bow'd down and pray'd for knighthood from the sword
Proved mortal to his house; for “ne'er again,”
Said he, “shall I encounter one so brave.”
Amid the surging bands he said the vow,
Received the hasty stroke; then with a rush
The two fair soldiers clave them out a path
To th' English centre and were overborne—
With all our host. 'Tis miserable news!
The streets are full of citizens grim-brow'd,
With rancour in their throats.
I like it not
That thus they are incensed; for in such mood
There's not a crime, however strange and black,
But they will hang it on their rulers' necks
To make a shame at which to point and jeer.
It carries danger, as your grace conceives,
And much I fear what other news may come.
Ay, Lindsey, there's the peril's very head.
We must be firm and stablish'd in our looks,
And in our speech most sad and circumspect.
Yon is Ramorgny, and the messenger
I sent upon his heels to slay the men
Who did the deed that never must be known.
Good news from Falkland? When returns the prince?
Never!
A most impossible, loathed word!
Colour your ashen cheeks, you raving fool!—
What, in my castle do you say he died?
It was a sort of dysent'ry, your grace.
Oh, if it were!—his face impeach'd my soul,
A keen, malignant, bitter, cursing face—
Have they yet buried him?
Your grace, they have,
With private ceremonial.
Where? where?
Lindores.
And there he lies with the quick fiends
Bound in his stony clay—
Tame your wild face!—
Fronting this doom I stand so terror-struck
That wail and grief are cow'd as childish things
Before an elder agitatiòn.
The king!
I dare not think.—
The prince is dead.
What, the dear prince!
The kind young prince!
Our mate!
His spirit pass'd away that stormy night.
Did he die hard?
Why?
No, 'twas short and fierce,
A feverous infection.
Prison-caught?
Oh, the poor king!
Mine eyes are wilful, Ralph.
I loved him. An' he'll drink a rouse no more.
Our days are over.
We'd best go repent;
For there's no liveliness in any sin,
Or chink of coin within our company.
I'll treat thee to a flagon for his sake.
An' while our throats are moist we'll pipe a mass.
Nay, pardie; but we'll give the priest his cup,
And set him to the chanting.
Come your way.
This is the very hour my brother stirs.
He will be here anon, and who will speak?
Not I, your grace.
Nor I, by my lost soul.
Nor I, for all the worth of very life.
Varlet!
The torture shall not move my lips.
Death shall not force my tongue to utterance.
Ruin and exile shall not ope my mouth.
Then must I do 't.
You must, your grace.
And will.
We humbly pray you.
How my flesh is thrill'd
And my speech curdles. Let me face the deed
One moment and grow strong—then bury it
Beneath the soil of consciousness so deep
The death-bed quake alone can rive the sod
That over-presses it. With this resolve
I have built up my fortitude—I will.

div.stage: [Enter King Robert, Prince James, and the Duchess Marjorie.]

lg.l: O woe is me for a defeated king!
In vain they changed my name from woful John
To favour'd Robert—vainly was it done.
Ye are all silent. Is it fond respect
To hoary shame and vanquish'd royalty?
No wonder that your brows are black to-day.
It is the mournful badge of minds bereaved.
Many the dead to mourn.
One more, my liege.
Is my son well?
Ay, as we count it bless'd.
Not dead?
Sweet majesty, at peace with God.
Dead, dead! You tell an old man he is dead.
I've look'd on in a cradle—who was full
Of light and movement—when? Whom I begot.
Help, help! I'm sinking!—Whither? To the depths
To find him who for evermore is gone?—
No end to where I sink!
A pillow here!
Raise up his head—this is unmanly grief,
Tho' eloquent for pardon. Chafe his hands.
We'll keep a silence till the fit is pass'd.
Oh, I shall never find him. I have gone
To deepest depths of Hell and utmost space—
For higher there's no warranty to go.—
Still he may be at Falkland.
Brother, no.
At Lindores is he buried.
Put from sight!—
God help my unbelief!
Be still. He prays.
When did he die?
The night of the great storm.
Of what complaint?
A fever.
And you said
He's buried?
Stop this catechism! Stop!
A king's command. She's had no offspring—she!
None.
Allan, ask them if he died a-bed,
Or on the floor as he had been a dog,
Who was my first begotten?
There was straw.
Shut his vile mouth!
Control this lawless grief.
How dare you speak who sway'd my anxious love
With sly, Satanic counsel; you who drew
The net you forced me spin about his life;
You who, miscall'd my brother, art my foe,
A murderer, false witness. 'Twas your speech
Beguiled my fatherhood; 'twas in your fort,
Your nest of bloodshed, that my son breathed out
The last of his short days. Traitor, begone!
I read you through and through.
I will not stay.
My pride instructs me, till this rage is out,
To spare my ill-starr'd, guiltless presence. Thus
I take my leave, till calmer thoughts shall claim
A penitent recall. Be comforted.
A hard-mouth'd, shallow wish! O Albany,
'Tis but the sword's point that is in my heart;
All the long cruel blade has yet to cut.
I know not how to grieve; but time to come
Will find me perfect at it. This is strange,
That all my sorrow is but prophecy.
Could he but weep!
Curses on Albany!
The traitor! murderer! our prince, our lord!
My David, thou wilt never be a king.
God lets me put that little strip of balm
About my bleeding love. It falls on thee,
My last, last son, the whelming heritage,
On thee, who still art mine! Here, to my breast,
And let it feel possession—carry it,
And crush it into permanence!
He weeps.
The red grief stains his lids.
Thou shalt not go,
As went thy brother. Oh, to think he's dead!
Within his fair and newly-fashion'd case
The pendulum of life no longer moves;
His face no longer answers to the hours,
Marking with lips and eyes their various flight;
Time has no mirror in his countenance;
There is no voice in him to sound its lapse;
The cunning clock of his mortality
Is stopp'd for ever, and my heart hath lost
The count of all her days.
Oh, do not weep!
Not till I have my privacy. I'll go
Straight to my inner chamber. Allan, come,
Whom I must burthen with this grievèd frame.
Well I believe that Albany is false.
He never loved the prince. I've deadly fear
That there hath been foul play. Oh, if there has
'Twill be reveal'd; for sin doth ever blab
And show the woman thro' its darkest crafts.
To think that all our merriment is done,
Our youth closed up and seal'd; our comrade gone
To lie beneath the ground where we must go.
How fares the king?
But just beyond the door
He fell at once into a second faint,
And so was borne to bed, where now he lies
As if extinct. I am suspicious, Walt.
Let's go and hear what rumour holds the crowd.

div.head: Scene I.
div.stage: —Edinburgh: Room in the Monastery of Holy Cross. Enter Walter and Allan.

lg.l: His grace of Albany will soon be here;
He comes to be acquitted by the king
Of any share in God's prerogative—
A natural death.
Keep down thy bitter voice;
No man creates a fever.
Not so sharp!
I think thy speech is full as sour as mine;
Man cannot starve his fellow; he's too soft
And pitiful for that.
Oh whisper me,
If you must blab street tales.
No fear to speak
What opes the general lip and blanches it.
Think you, mine Allan, that the king hath heard
How all men say his elder son was slain.
Ay, Walt; he will not eat until we name
Prince James; then shudders through his ancient form,
And groans within the hollow of his chest,
“Starved, starved!” I never knew so large a grief.
You lose the man within his sorrow's might.
Oh, here he comes, as if he'd slept in tombs.
Poor royal father!
Everything prepared.
I think my brother will not keep me long;
I'm troubled that I spake so hastily
To one of my own blood; it raises fear,
And makes my conscience feverish and ill,
To think how I accused him in my wrath.
It cannot be; I ever found him kind.
And his high office breeds in common souls
Tale-bearing envy.—You once served my son,
If I mistake not?
Sire, I loved him well.
Allan, this knave shall wait on me—you two
Who both have loved my son.—D' you know, last night
I dreamt of him. Within the monast'ry
Of far Lindores I saw the straight cold tomb,
And the straight form—all the round lines of youth,
The full serenity of cheek and chin
Cut clearer in the moonlight's marble mould;
The brow a blank page of the whitest peace;
Yet round about twirled a dim company,
Grey sprites of Famine, shaking poppy-stems
And stalks of corn that wagged their lavish heads,
Deriding the lean body underneath
Its effigy, that still and satisfied
Lay close against the wall. God! to that tomb
My love is pilgrim—with my heart's red drops
Telling an awful penance.
My dear lord,
And new kind master, do not ever dwell
On such grim churchyard thoughts. We've heaven and bliss.
I cannot yet go further than the tomb;
There lies the ruined body that I built,
The fair new city where I sent my hopes,
Carrying fire from my own shrine of life
To settle and increase. Yet I, even I,
Put out the hearth and overthrew the home
And pierced the very heart of my desires.
His grace your brother comes. You'll take your seat
Upon the dais yonder, whereto flock
The people of your household; see!
I live
Within this painted nothingness—this world
That stares into mine eyes and holds them not,
This insolent, vain show.
We'll stand aside.

div.stage: [Enter Albany, Lindsey, and other Nobles with their trains.]

lg.l: My liege, I break your meditation
For nothing less than honour, for amends
To stabbed and bleeding innocence, yourself
Have wounded first and foremost. These, your lords,
My peers and gracious equals, do acquit
My dear renown from stain of that dread crime
Whose breath would smirch my whiteness. Parliament,
After all due enquiry, strictest search,
And earnest fanning of the fearful charge,
Hath found it chaff, as these can testify.
My liege, we can.
There is no evidence.
We frankly own him guiltless of this sin.
Thus we accept him with our penitence.—
O Robert!
Sir, I'd have you quite convinced.
I'd be impregnable in pardon. Think!
Without a motive stronger than herself,
Would Nature so unnatural become
As spill her proper blood? That so she would
Is beyond all belief. In motive lies
Sole credit to my having done the deed
That seared me in your favour. First my love—
Which, though the chastisement its care advised,
Was turned of God to doom, thereby received
No taint or flaw in truth—my blood-knit love
Long-shown is strong 'gainst the ambitious thought
That I am charged withal. One royal branch
Clipt from the golden tree of monarchy
Leaves yet another in his crescent bloom—
He's looking at the boy with eagle eye—
It is a look of seizure!—O my James,
Come to your father's arms!
See where he grows
From the old noble trunk. Ambition gives
No slightest motive.
'Tis enough. You're clear.
That all my love was mocked by the event
Is sore to think on. Who can trammel Death
With cords obedient to mortal will?
My castle hath no dungeon that would hold
Th' invisible last foe. For his offence,
Which God's great judgment-day alone can strike,
I as a man must suffer, while unscathed
Goes the arch-murderer of hope and joy.
It is most true. I'm sorry in my heart
That I accused you from an unchecked mouth.
Most true! Death oft makes innocence seem guilt.
Forgive me, Robert.
Nay, I have no need.
'Twas natural that you should doubt, suspect,
Where circumstance so darkly pointed out;
And grief 's a headstrong unenlightened guide.
I knew that reason, toiling through the mists
Of sorrowful opinion and blind wrath,
Would show me white and shine on me again
Whom passion over-clouded. I am blessed
In daylight of your favour. That report
That stirs among the commoners, and sinks
Into base hearts against me, that I starved—
God's sake, no more!
That villainous, black tale
Gains credit from the rumour'd cruelty
To England's second Richard. He whom Death
With still and sudden handling carries home,
Forsooth! upon the people's oath, is starved.
If you will have acquittal, pardon, grace,
Strangle within your throat that awful word,
And never freeze the aching man in me
With such inhuman, foul suggestion.
O God! that ever such a thing hath been
Cries shame upon Thy fatherhood—unless
Thou leav'st the punishment of children's sin
To devils of the pit. O God! O God!
The anguish burns me—shrivels up my soul
To whitened ashes and blank lifelessness.
The king is moved.
Unhappy that I am,
Pleading for pardon, that my tongue should blast
Where it would run to heal. I only spoke
To shut your doors of hearing from the sound
Of false alarum to your tender love;
And lo! I wake the sentries of your soul
To naked panic. Brother, dearest liege,
Have pity on my lips' mistake—forgive!
Whereas I feel that none who shares my blood,
Or of my mother drank the gentle milk,
Could within utmost limits of belief
Descend from man to monster—at this time,
Here in this place, I do acquit thy hand
Of murder pitiless, thy thought of stain
From black, disnatured treason, and thy soul—
Go, take it to the certain eye of God,
Not to the tear-dimmed vision of a man,
Thine earthly king and brother. Nevermore
Speak of this matter,—'tis my earnest pray'r.
So much of pain it brands upon my thought,
Silence alone can cicatrize the wound.
Poor brother—here's my hand!
I kiss it, sir.
Lo! the remission for our liege to sign,
In Latin writ, which clears my innocence
And that of Archibald of Douglas, which
Hath suffered slur with mine.
A pen!
You're free.—
Oh! with a pen I made him prisoner!
What counsel would you take with these your lords?
You summoned us to conference, my liege.
I'd not forgotten. It is near our heart.—
Leave us, my James; go to our rooms awhile,
Where I can find you presently—my room.—
Our words concern our heir and only son.
He is a forward scholar and hath learnt
All that our northern wisdom can impart,
Alas! but little worth, to Scotland's shame.
Learning is not less golden in a king
Than his own crown; and manners grace him more,
As he can more display them in his rank,
Than those beneath his sway; we therefore dream
Of foreign education for our son
In polished France.
Sooth to my very aim!
My liege, 'tis prudent and well-reasoned.
Yes.
I'm glad it meets your will. The faithful Earl
Of Orkney will attend our dearest son
With chosen servants. Ere he sail from hence,
We would consult your lordships once again.
Now we would have our privacy.
We'll go;
And ever study to deserve your love.
Oh! it is done!
I've set my little boat upon wide seas
To save it from the jealous flames aboard
That scorch it for destruction. Allan, fetch
The Earl of Orkney hither.
Kindly knave,
Come tell me, I'm a cruel father? Ay?
Oh, not so cruel as the circumstance
You'd ward off from your son.
How? You are dim.
I wish men spoke their minds with meaning clear.
I'm an old man and my conception slow.
I meant that many dangers threaten him
Who is sole heir to sovereignty—no more.
That was not it.—Good fellow, do you think
That I shall live to see my son return?
O sire, you're hale in body.
But the heart—
D' you think that it can hold such space of time?
With patience, yes!

sp.speaker: King Robert.

lg.l: With passion—no! Then there is memory,
And all this mourning we must add thereto.

sp.stage: [Enter the Earl of Orkney and Allan.]

lg.l: Good earl, 'tis settled that you go with him.
Thank Heaven that you live whom I can trust.
You will be very watchful; if he die,
I am an old and childless man, an end,
A mortal Omega, a mere life's term,
And ancient monument to Hope's defeat.
My liege, I will protect him, watch and love
With upright loyalty and perfect care.
Why do you weep so bitterly, my liege?
O Allan, 'tis a very bitter thought
That turns my tears to Marah. O my son!
'Twill grieve him sore to part with you.
Of him
I was not thinking. He is true and fair,
But very young, and he will soon forget.
Storms crush the bearded grain; 'twill never rise.
The tender sprouting blade is dashed, but springs
The better for its grief.—Your arm, kind earl.
There's much to settle, many things to do
Before you start. We'll walk together, earl.
We'll to his chamber, Walt, and gladden it
With sun and air and cleansing.
'Tis high time,
For like a bat's nest hath it been of late.
His absence is our opportunity.
Go, fetch the prior.
I will, your grace.
At once.
I'll wait him here. I cannot sleep at night;
Dreams enter when I close my eyes, and stalk
Along the silent passages of thought
Like ghosts. My health is touched. This must not be.
Rest is a precious store I cannot spend
On vanities and filmy toys of fear.
This prior shall obtain for me from Rome
A pardon that will lay my haunting crime
With sacred exorcism. Here he comes.
Hail.
Benedicite!
So would I were,
Yet scarcely live I blessed, with dark reports
So cast within the mirrors of my soul
That she is well-nigh blinded to herself,
And takes the dirt that's thrown as native filth
And dregs of her impurity. I scarce
Believe that I am Albany—so vile,
Corroded, monstrous, full of subtle sin,
My enemies declare me. You have heard
That Parliament has clarified my fame,
The king declared my spotlessness and health.
You think I have enough restored my soul?
No; there's the holy Church I grieved with guilt
Apparent. I would have her pardon, claim
Exoneration from the weight of crime
Which those who freely hate me still would heap
On my bewildered innocence. I ask
This right, that she establish me in faith,
In guiltlessness, and loyalty.
Your grace,
Why need you pardon where there's no offence?
To fortify from slander. Those that brag
Against my newly washed, unsullied name,
As if it once were black, will lose their tongue
When they shall find any untoward speck
Of former misconception, error, fault,
Which no man, by his nature, can escape,
Is cleared by holy Church.
Your grace takes note
Too closely of the swarms that sting your name
With wounds ephemeral. Such ever fret
The ease of reputation.
Pardon me.
I suffer from no pricks, but trenchèd scars.
The brand of Cain, the infamous red curse,
Is struck across the brow of my repute.
'Twill blush the more if pardoned. To forgive,
Where sin is absent, fills the emptiness
With sin's own lurid stain.
Not so, not so.
It is a measure of state-policy
To silence evil tongues.
To teach them words
Of stablished calumny.
There you misjudge.
I know men better. Obloquy is dumb
Before the vindication of the Church.
I'd have you write to Rome this very night,
And send a speedy messenger.
Take thought.
If, with a soilèd conscience you would steal
The balm that heals confession into peace,
Great were your condemnation.
Priest, you tread
Too near our honour. Am I not declared
By the vox populi—the voice of God—
In parliament, and by my peers, unblamed,
Unblameable?
You are.
And by the king
Acknowledged sinless?
Yes, you are.
What more
Desire you?
That your lips should firmly seal
The clean page of denial with the stamp
And image of your soul.
You ask for much.
No Christian dares to say he hath no sin.
Your peers declared you sinless, so you plead.
Will you accept the declaration?
No.
The declaration for the special sin
That's laid to your account?
You pry too far.
Go, write the letter. I disdain to speak
The answer to suspicion.
I will write.
I know not if His Holiness will grant
The pardon you desire.
Nay, urge him to 't,
As I am rich and great within the land.
Not so, your grace, as you are innocent;
A bribe would but unsettle the belief
That you are pure of murder. The clean hand,
Unreddened by the stain of blood, as much
Detests the golden taint of proffered coin.
Dishonoured is the honour that is bought.
You wrong me. I but said that as I'm great,
Pre-eminent in riches, which are snares
Fate spreads for Envy's watching, it were best
I should be fortified with clear renown
And holy recognition. By the death
Of the king's son, I'm Regent—at the point
And pinnacle of influence. A slur
Cast on my faith, looses the bond of trust
That girdles monarchy;—rank treason spreads
Among the scattered members, social craft,
Domestic infidelity, the guile
Of business, and the tricks of usury.
His Holiness will never thus dissolve
The unity of State, and strike the Church
With such unsanctified and rude assault
To manners and religion. Put this down
Within the letter, using choicer phrase
Selected by your learning.
I will write.
God knows I'd have your grace unsullied.
Write
This very eve.
I will.—Contrition makes
Appeal far surer than my feeble pen.
Your pen be strong! To-morrow I'll to shrift.
Why do you pause?
Acknowledgment is grace.
Go to!—I'd have you purge disloyalty,
Pardon foul lips, detraction infamous.
I would forgive my enemies in thus
Securing false forgiveness for myself.
Mac Louis!
Show the prior out. Return.
This will establish peace within my breast.
Oh, may it pacify the corpse of him
Who cannot sleep at Lindores! It is said
That prodigies make eloquent his tomb,
And call for blood to still the murdered soul
With slumber of accomplished Nemesis.
My blood he asks—mine, or my children's blood.
If not my blood, then theirs! Not theirs, not theirs!
Child of my brother, O avenging ghost,
As thou wert young, ask not my children's blood,
And cut not off my seed, though such a doom
Were perfect justice! I must wait my time;
So must they wait. We know not here nor there,
How, when, requital comes; but if besought
Thus from the bed of stone where murder lies,
Its coming is secure. And yet I think
These miracles are old wives' tales—no more.
Guilt blurs my understanding. Twice to-day
I stumbled,—when I named my crime aloud
Before the king, and when I offered gold
For Church's pardon. Twice the cloud hath swept
My brain's clear weather. But here comes a gleam
Of goodly sun—that James is bound for France.
It promises the mid-day of my fame,
The perfect shining of my dearest hope.
I'll sleep on it.
To-night I'll have strong drink—
A posset! Bring it to my sleeping-room.

div.head: Scene II.
div.stage: —A Chamber. King Robert, Prince James, and the Earl of Orkney.

lg.l: The convoy waits his highness.
Rather say
That dangers wait him; harsh, ambitious seas,
And pulseless rocks and unrelenting winds.
The elements are homeless, unallied;
They have no bonds, no sanctities. I've watched
All day the West imbrued with sable storm.
I think the breeze is higher.
Nay. I'll swear
Its freshness hath declined.
Good! Then we'll wait
Till all the air is motionless and safe.
Tarry no more, my liege. To slowly part
Doth make the rift of parting an abyss.
O earl, I cannot heave up from my heart
Its anchor with Farewell!
Yet must you part.
Not yet—not yet! I cannot loose at once;
With soft persistence must the minutes work,
Or I shall die.
Father!
My only child!
Last leaf of my sere bough, when once I loose
Thy bond of dear reliance from my side,
Untraversable space cuts in between,
And I am bare for ever.
Come, my liege,
You speak as journey never had return,
And Providence were nought.
A keen rebuke!
God has a human family, and I
Have but one mortal son.—Oh, let me look,
Gaze at your face and see the future in 't.
I shall not watch its changes—never seize
The gracious steps whereby your favours mount
To manhood's comely top. Your brother's face
Was far more delicate, the lips more full
And chafing, and the brow less wide and free,
With less of gentle space between the eyes
As frank as yours. It was a face that drew
Much love, except when temper blasted it,
Or scorn envenomed. You are sweetly tuned,
An even nature; on your forehead dreams,
And empire on your mouth. You'll be a man
Beneficent and royal. Check those sobs.
If I am dead, my spirit will rejoice.
I cannot leave you.
Child, nor I loose you.
And yet I must, if in the barren world
My flesh would still have aught to call its own.
Go!—nay, but wait! You'll think of me at night,
The games and studies done—think how I lie
And ponder you. To Memory, as God,
The darkness and the light are both alike.
I'll say “good-night,” and leave the southern winds
To give it to the northern.
I shall pray,
And plunge your name into a well of tears
To send it washed to Heaven.
I will kiss
My hand to you ere sleeping.
And you'll love
The rude land of your birth, nor jest at it?
I've got some heath to carry into France;
They say at Paris it is never seen.
A bushy lock clipt from your country's brow,—
Join it with this from my white forehead ta'en.
Be faithful to the twisted memories.
And, James, there is a head as bright as yours
That's laid beneath the ground. Remember it;
James, James, remember how your brother died.
I will—when I am king.
I know thou wilt.
The close lips are an oath.
My liege, time runs.
The hour-glass of my very fatherhood
Shows all its moments gone. I cannot say
The dire word that bereaves me; once I signed
A warrant ... Earl, no torture man conceives
Could crush this centre down;—God has a rack
Whereon He breaks some hearts.—I keep you, earl.
My child,
One mighty speechless clasp! Thus, thus, begot,
Thus lost for ever to my arms' embrace. ...
Now falls the stroke—now, now!
I'll run away.
Settle thy chin nor weep. All's over now.
James, send me all the verses that you write;
Your masters' names and how you spend each day;
And who is kind and if the land is fair.
He's gone! Good earl, go after! Shut the door.
Starved, starved! Starvation! David, David! Son!
It's in my heart the hunger and the want,
And from the lenten depths of my own soul
I pity thee. And—oh!—to think of it!
His vivid youth and golden beauty gone
To the unloved Obscure, the comfortless
Environment of Night. I know they think
That I forget him; for his memory
That like a grave-stone stood against my heart
Hath sunk into its substance, and now seems
To careless eyes half lost; but so much more
'Tis hidden in my love's dark sepulchre.
He gave his lusty years to wantonness
And shameful riot. All my being's hope
I'd give for his deliverance. And yet
I did not train him with strict uprightness;
I gave my precepts with a fearful voice,
O'erlook'd his irreligion, made excuse
For spotted innocence and growing guilt.
He died in soul. My brother married him
With gross dishonour—so he died in heart.
I left his punishment in other hands;
And then he died in body; triple death,
Three-fold starvation! I am judged. Ah me!
And yet I send my sole surviving child
To a licentious court, that I may shun
His arduous protection. God is just.
I who have loosed all duties from my neck,
Shall sometime feel the stone of Sisyphus
Rolled on to me for carriage. Yet—O God!—
The stranger's care alone could save my child.
My son and grandsons in a vision bowed
Their heads before me, and my phantom-hand
Let fall the hungry steel upon their necks.
My sin, my sin was executioner,
For I myself was dead as midnight ghost.—
All this is fever; yet within the lines
Of sane and irreproachable surmise
My fear attains to danger; for my son
Is feeble, indolent,—a man of peace,
Unworthy of my loins; he'll lose my gain,
Drop what I've damned my soul to lay on him.
Then is there James. ... Would he might share
His brother's grave! A like captivity
Shall wither him—
Your grace, Sir John is dead.
Ramorgny? He hath lived
A white and staring life these many days.
How ended it?
He hung against the wall
Within a dusty corner.
Self-undone.
'Twas melancholia!—Attend my charge
Go: bear this letter to the English king.—
Here is a purse.—Rest not, until you lay
Its sealèd sheet within his royal hand.
My bounteous lord, this opportunity
To do you service—
Speak not; but begone.
O Opportunity!—
My soul, self-murdered, rots beneath the stake
That pointed her direction. Now again
She glimmers on the crooked, deep-cut way
Of treachery, and I will follow her.
She is the fleeting guide that draws my life
Through all its paths of darkness; she's the star
That leads ambition forth! My letter greets
The King of England, tells him how the seas
Are bringing James to France, sets down the points
Where he will touch on English ground, and when.
The lure will take; my last impediment
Find, like my first, a prison. I am blessed.
Would that the pardon came, and that I felt
Less sick at banquets, and saw less of dreams.

div.head: Scene IV.
div.stage: —The Castle of Rothsay in Bute. A Chamber. King Robert, the Duchess Marjorie, Allan.

lg.l: Now that my infamous, false bond is loosed,
And death has cleared my wrong, with sweetened thought
I tend and love my monarch's broken age.
My pride no longer fills my care with gall
As when his son was living.—Let me put
Your cushion smooth and easy for the head.—
Good Allan, help me.
Blank—no gratitude.
His agèd sight is travelling across
The limit whence his life will follow it.
He listens to our human speech no more
Than if his ears were closed. He cannot last
More than to learn his son is safe in France.
Ha! France!
Yes, sire—Prince James is surely safe.
The wind hath favour'd sailing.
Let me raise
Your feet, my father, on this other stool.
He's gone again.
A lost, a feeble face
That makes no terms with Death.
Lady, I'm glad
That I have had no children. It is sore
To lose them—see them die like upward sparks,
And your own embers burning still to ash.
Yes—and to see them sin and sell their souls
To vanity. I'll never give the world
More lives to waste.
An' yet to have no love!
I loved your husband; I had been forlorn
Without his kindly laugh.
Enough! He died
In time to save his kindness from all taint,
But nothing else.
Look! Does the weather-cock
Still point to south?
Yes, and the day is fair
And full of shining.
Help me to look out.
You are too weak to move.
I must look out.
Support me to the window.—Over there
Is France, the sunny land, beyond those fields
Of wheaten green, beyond, beyond, beyond!
And where's the east?
'Tis yonder.
Over there
Is dark Lindores, beyond the blasted moors
That make the distance mourn—beyond, beyond!
Both unattainable! O heart, too far!—
Now I'll sit down.—Why runs that man so fast?
Perchance he brings us happy tidings, sire,
That the young prince is well.
My tongue hath swooned
At presage of his tidings. Haste—O stay—
Not more ... I should be stronger tasting death
To bear it. ...
Nay, 'tis surely happy news.
Our gallant prince in health and full of joy.
Look! they are come. What ho! Prince James is safe!

div.stage: [Enter the Earl of Buchan and Walter.]

lg.l: He's in an English prison—in the Tow'r
That frowns upon the Thames. King Henry hath,
Against the laws of knighthood, seized the ship
That bore our prince, and vows he'll teach the tongue
Of France to Scotland's heir.
He's dead.
No, no:
In prison, and a kindly one they say.
He's dead—he's dead! They told me such false tales;
David was but in prison, in kind walls—
And he was dead. I'm near the grave for lies
To much avail you.
No; he is not dead.
He's well and treated in most gracious ways.
Starved?
He is well attended and well kept,
Even from the royal board.
Away, begone!
I'm dying, and you thrust the earth on me.
I'm on my way to judgment. Let me face
No witnesses;—no bleeding chiefs that slew
Each other, I consenting; no poor souls
I've left to evil men; no innocents
Condemned by wicked judges I have feared
To thwart; no beggars, stripped by greedy lords
Whose avarice I bore; no murdered forms
Whose murd'rers I forgave. No need of such.
I plead that I am guilty.—Bring them not.
I'm guilty on my solemn oath, O God.
Father of men, King of the universe,
I've sinned in Thy great offices—in both!
Bring not Thy witnesses—my people's ghosts.
Bring not that dear dread witness, with pale hands
And different keen face and eyes, whose look
Would fix a root of horror in my soul
To grow up like a yew-tree from a grave.
Let me be judged within an empty court!
Or, if we're judged together,—when the book
Is opened, where in lines of red are writ
The sins of his few years,—
And he stands far apart in white despair,
Then shall he answer to a few that fall
From the accusing lips, but point the sum
To me for answer. I will take them all
As blessings:—for a father's sins extend
Far over his own blotted page; yea, fill
With scarlet of damnation many blanks
His children had left clean except for him.
How solemn is this judgment before death,
Enacted for our profit.
Thus to see
A soul in flesh corruptible appear
Before th' immortal bar.
My God, my God!
I wait Thy sentence; I am self-contemned,
Without a word from any human voice.
It will not be to flames! Some writers say
The punishments of hell are nothing more
Than change of states—each man his opposite.
If so, then I shall be a childless slave,
My fatherhood and royalty displaced,
Seen in some other, who within my sight
Leans his one hand upon a goodly son,
The other on a sceptre. Then, oh then,
The penal fires would be like Heaven's glow,
Their smoke refreshing cloud and covering
From the heart-scorching sight.
Will none approach
To hold him up?
I will.—His eyes are wild
With something in the depths.
Lost! lost! 'Tis done.
There is no crown upon my head. Oh say,
Is nothing on my head?
A little round
Of sovereign gold.
But I can feel there's naught;
And in me all my father's love is sucked
Forth by the cruel wind.—What face is that?
I never knew it. Yet the hair—the hair!
But oh! the eyes—I've never looked on such,
Nor known those lips. If it should be my son,
I do disown him, disinherit, curse!
Now Hell receive me!
See, the change hath come,
Death's ashen tread, before it stoops to take.
Gather about him now the strife is done.
Peace presses us together.
Prison! Death!
The cloud of night is rising in mine eyes;
I feel Life turn the key upon my heart.
There is no op'ning.—It is dark—I die.
That was the last heave of the broken heart,
The last breath of the soul.
My king, my lord!
I never thought thy death would be so strange,
With all that pain to end a gentle life.
Your grace, the king is dead.
How!—dead!—the king!
He died upon the news that James is ta'en
The King of England's captive.
Now your grace
Is Regent, till the prisoner is loosed,
Whose chains bind down our restive fealty
And tie it to your will.
A trust I hold
But for the regal future. Lift the head!
Died he at peace?
Oh no, he mourn'd his son
Till we could hear no more.
Alas! and this
Is rule and monarchy—to be like this,
Poor, old, unhappy, ignorant, extinct.—
For this I've doom'd my soul. What's done is done.
I'll use my fortune till I'm even thus.—
He had few sins to dread.
And yet he died
Most full of hellish terrors.
I will send
A great procession. John, I mourn thy fate.
False was the comfort that new-nam'd thy state.
I'll to a convent's refuge, there to pray
For his affrighted soul, and sooth to say
For his sake will I join another name
To his and never think they're not the same.
His heart was broken, not by strokes of Time,
But thrusts of him who should have propp'd it. Crime
Such as dark Albany's is visited
On the third generation. Raise the dead.
His doom was in his gentleness and fear.
His changèd name still brought him to this bier.
